I think that I have trouble sleeping two to three times a week, which, like I said, is rather strange

The strangest thing, though, is how often my mind just seems to go blank.
I'll be doing something such as a puzzle, and then just totally lose track of where I am and what I'm doing.
Have you had any other incidents like this? Where you become confused?
Yes, I had an episode the other day. I went to the hardware store to pick up a few tools for a project.
Some strange man came up to me and started chit-chatting about something about my old company.
I had no idea who this person was, but it was clear he knew me, and had worked with me.
I later worked out he had worked as an intern in my department a few years before.
That was when I started to realise that I was having problems recognising people, if
I met them outside of where I was accustomed to seeing them.

recognising people?
I sometimes get quite irritated with people.
It feels like my mind does not have the ability
to work out what is going on in a situation
before everything changes.

for something simple, like chair.

Not all that much, unfortunately.
I always envisioned my golden years walking the dog and playing with my grandchildren.
But nowadays I rarely leave the house.
So there is a lack of exercise?
Okay, and any health problems such as cardiovascular disease?
Yes, I take one tablet a day for high blood pressure.
I started taking them about five years ago I think.
Mr Jones, we will have to run some additional tests,
tests, but it appears that you may be experiencing early onset dementia. You have told me about
a number of risk factors such as cardiovascular disease, a low level of physical activity,
and several years of sleep disturbance.
Is dementia serious? Or will it just make me forget things now and then? I mean it seems
as though everybody has it nowadays.
Dementia is a terminal disease in the long term. In fact, it's the second leading cause
of death in Australians. Yes, you will start to be more forgetful, but it is also a brain
disorder that has a negative impact on thinking, behaviour and the performance of everyday tasks.
Dementia is an umbrella term for up to 200 different conditions, so we will need to do
some additional work to identify your particular problems. For example, you describe difficulty
recognizing faces, which indicates prosopagnosia. You also mention sometimes feeling frustrated
because you are unable to pause and reflect on what is going on around you.
Is there anything I can do to help slow the symptoms?
We need to increase your level of physical activity and get you sleeping better.
This will improve your overall health as well as deal with some of these risk
crackers directly related to dementia.
How does sleep affect my brain?
It affects it in a number of ways. Sleep works like a sewage system for the brain. As you
sleep it clears out toxic chemicals and proteins that are involved in different types of dementia.
One question that Mr Jones, when you do fall asleep do you wake up a lot?
Yes I do. Also my wife often has to jostle me to wake me up as she says I often stop breathing
while I'm asleep. I used to take sleeping tablets but I don't like the way they made
me feel so I stopped.
Mmm, that is quite common in older people. You see, what happens when you stop breathing
is that your brain is not getting the oxygen it needs. This is extremely detrimental for
your memory. Also, when you sleep well, your brain is able to create new neurons, a process
called neurogenesis. When you experience chronic sleep disruption, you impair this process and others
that are important for reducing inflammation in your body. The good news is that with early
intervention it is possible to slow the disease course. As to the sleeping tablets, I would not
suggest them for the long term. They are fine for about of poor sleep but I don't recommend
them to be used for more than two weeks. There are some behavioural techniques and cognitive
behavioral psychological techniques for sleep disturbance.
A referral to a specialist that I work with often is what I'm going to recommend now.

nearly twice as much as she should have been taking. Was the pain medication actually helping

What side effects were you experiencing?
I didn't know at the time, but I had quite a few side effects.
The most serious was severe constipation and nausea.
There were days when I didn't want to leave the house because of it.
The medication also affected my mood quite a lot.
I felt low and I became withdrawn.
No friends, no social events.
I even contemplated suicide at one point.
How about memory loss or fuzziness?
I have had a couple of episodes of memory loss. I remember one time I was on my way to
work from dropping my son off at uni and I couldn't remember which route to take. Then
I started to feel paranoid, like everyone was noticing that I was lost. So I started
to drive fast and get ahead of the traffic. Then I was afraid of getting stopped by the
police, so I started to drive very slowly. That is when I knew I was a danger and needed
to do something to get my life back. That was two months ago.
How long between when you started taking painkillers and that incident with your memory?
Ten years.
Did any of the doctors that you see during that time suggest you cut down on your pain
killers?
No, not until I changed GPs. My new GP told me that many of the symptoms I was reporting,
like the nausea and memory loss, were side effects of the painkillers no one had ever told me
that before.
And not that surprise. There's little guidance and support at the moment for GPs to help
people to taper off their opioids safely and be able to manage their pain using non-drug
techniques. For many years doctors were trained to give opioids to people in pain.
Yes, that's what my current GP told me.
We have developed a package of care that involves a multi-pronged approach. The first phase involves
three days with especially trained nurse. You will learn about what opioids are, how they
work in terms of pain, and the nurse will start to give you drug-free pain management
techniques. Then you will move on to your group. During group work, you will learn stress
management techniques such as learning to use relaxation as well as cognitive behavioural
approaches, which involves changing your thinking patterns and putting in place goals for yourself.
After the group element of the program, you will start to have a one-to-one session with
a nurse who will generate a tapering plan to help you reduce your intake of opioids.
This nurse will serve as a point of contact once you leave the intensive phase of treatment.
Well, what about withdrawal?
We understand that pain medication is a safety net for a lot of people.
That is why we have the nurse who will work with you on your tapering plan.
Okay, I'm quite worried about my pain after the treatment.
How will I manage it without my education?
Actually what's interesting is that drugs like opioids may not be all that effective for long-term pain like back pain.
Our treatment plan will help you to learn other techniques to deal with the chronic pain.

Hello everyone, it's an incredible honour to be here today.
I'm Alan Jackson, a radiologist and researcher with Imperial College London.
I'm here to present Breakthrough Research on the use of artificial intelligence in reading
mammogram scans.
This research was conducted with a team of researchers at my institution, as well as other
research institutions across the United Kingdom, in collaboration with Google, a company I'm
sure everyone is very familiar with.
Just to give a little background about how mammogram scans are currently read, the system
that the National Health Service, better known as the NHS, uses two radiologists to analyze
each woman's mammogram scans.
Think about that for one second. All women in England between the ages of 47 and 73 are
invited by the NHS to have a mammogram every three years. Getting back to my original point,
occasionally a third doctor is called in to assess the images, when the first two cannot
come to an agreement. Another important fact to keep in mind about the current system of
diagnosis of breast cancer is that the number of years of training that radiologists need
in order to interpret mammograms is more than 10, which is quite an investment of time and
resources for both the individual and the NHS. This lengthy specialised training is partially
responsible for an estimated shortage of more than 1,000 radiologists across the United Kingdom.
Our research study using an AI or Artificial Intelligence Model
shows that artificial intelligence is as good as the system currently in use at diagnosing breast
cancer and there is actually a reduction of 1.2% in false positives as well as a reduction of 2.7%
1% in false negatives. A false positive is when a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer,
when in fact she does not have cancer, and a false negative refers to women who do have
cancer, but it is not detected at the time of the scan. The improvements possible with
AI mean that fewer women will be subjected to unnecessary and costly treatment, and more
All women who do need treatment will receive it.
The way that AI works to detect breast cancer in mammogram scans is through machine learning.
Machine learning involves computer algorithms that can learn and improve without being explicitly
told how.
This means that the algorithm will get better over time as it scans more and more images.
Researchers use x-ray images of breasts of former patients from government databases.
All images have been stripped of any personal information that could be used to identify
the patient.
Patients were initially concerned with a company like Google having access to their health
records, so this was key to protecting patient privacy and making them feel at ease with
this research project.
Doctors and the public in general may be wondering if this means that AI will take over from
human doctors.
The short answer is no. We are nowhere close to letting AI loose in the laboratory. Like
with any initial research project, it is still early and further research has to be done,
and even then, at least one specially trained radiologist would remain in charge of diagnosis.
This would mean that AI could help to do away with the need for two doctors to read
each scan, which in turn would ease the workload and free up radiologists to do even more important
things. It could also speed up diagnosis as the computer algorithm can analyze images within seconds
and also due to the fact that computers don't need rest as they don't get tired.
This will reduce wait times and worry for patients as well as increase the likelihood of positive
outcomes. This particular research project focused on women in the UK particularly because we had
ready access to millions of mammogram scans. The research team is looking to collaborate
with international partners so that this research can help clinicians around the world to make
more accurate diagnoses, leading to earlier detection and more successful interventions
for patients as the algorithm gets better and better.
I would like to thank you all for your attention as well as my research partners and institutions
here in the UK and our colleagues at Google for all the support. I will now take questions
from the audience.

Hello everyone. Thank you for the warm welcome. I'm so happy to be here today to tell you
about a very special patient of mine. My name's Sally Grasslait. I'm a thoracic surgeon at James
Cook University Hospital with over 15 years of experience. Came to know my patient, John Blake,
after he visited at least 10 general practitioners for his rare condition. John, I will let you tell
a little bit about your medical history before talking about my proposed treatment plan.
I have always felt self-conscious about my chest wall. When other boys were running
around the beach with their shirts off, I always kept my shirt on to hide my chest.
You see, the breastbone sinks in quite dramatically, which in addition to being a source of embarrassment
causes me to experience frequent breathlessness, fatigue, dizziness and accelerated heartbeat.
I can't do simple things like run up a hill or go on a hike because I can't breathe and
my heart is pumping blood so fast, I feel as though I might pass out.
The combination of my chest and the limitations that my condition put on my physical activity
definitely shaped my adolescence and early adulthood.
Over the years I started to see GP after GP.
doctor, grass lake already mentioned, it was at least 10 in all. At around the seventh
doctor, I finally got a name for my condition, Pectus Excavatum. But none of them was able
to tell me if my symptoms were caused by my condition. I knew in my heart, haha, there
was a link between the shape of my chest and my symptoms. But the doctors would not say
it out loud. It also turns out that by the time I got a name for my condition, the NIH
NHS no longer offers surgery for this condition, because it says there is insufficient evidence
of the benefits of surgical treatment. It is all incredibly frustrating.
As I became a teenager and later young adult, my condition and its effect on my quality
of life started to affect my mental health. This combined with my negative experience
with doctors meant that I started to isolate myself and withdraw from all social interaction.
I definitely did not act like your typical teen. I also started to take antidepressants.
That is when I sought out as specialist.
For me, it was quite clear that John's heart was being squashed by his sternum and that
this was causing his symptoms. In addition to what I could see on the scans, there was
no other plausible explanation for his symptoms. I mean, in all other respects, John is a
a healthy young man. As I have treated other patients with John's condition I was well
aware that there is a perfectly safe and routine treatment for this condition. The standard
treatment for Sunken Chest Syndrome or Pectus Excavatum is the NUS procedure, which is
a minimally invasive procedure that has been around since the late 1980s and involves placing
one or more metal bars to correct the shape of the chest, which in turn relieves pressure
on the heart. The number of bars depends on how severe the dip in the chest is. Generally,
the more severe the dip in the chest, the fewer bars fit. The NUS procedure is my recommendation
for his condition. The bars typically stay in place for 2-3 years before needing to be
removed and new bars inserted. One possible complication of the surgery is that the bars
will flip, which will result in quite a lot of pain for the patient. This complication
can be avoided by tackling the problem early in the patient's life, when the bone structure
is still forming. In addition to there being fewer complications, recovery time for the
procedure is reduced for smaller children as their bodies more easily adapt to the bars.
That is why it is particularly important for GPs and pediatricians to learn about this
condition because they are generally the first point of contact for young patients and their
families. In fact, the procedure was originally developed at a children's hospital.
Unfortunately, that was not an option for me because the GPs that I saw as a teenager
